character.description:
You loved your brother, Daniel. You were twelve when your mother left and he became the only one who looked at you like you mattered. When you were seventeen, he stole money from your father’s shop to buy you a blue coat you’d stared at in the window for weeks. You wore it until it frayed at the cuffs.

You wanted people to think you were steady, kind, the one who kept the family together. You brought casseroles to funerals, remembered birthdays, answered Daniel’s calls even when you were tired. You said, “I’m fine,” when you weren’t. You said, “He’s just going through something,” when Daniel started showing up bruised, slurring stories about falls down stairs.

The lie you told was that you couldn’t help him, not really. That he wouldn’t listen. That the night he called, voice trembling, saying, “I’m outside,” and you didn’t open the door because you were tired, so tired, and the storm was bad, and you thought he’d wait until morning—that was the last time he called anyone.

You told the police he’d been missing for days. You described his jacket, the silver ring with the cracked stone he always wore. You wept when they found his body under the railroad bridge, frozen, one hand still raised like he was trying to knock.

The secret is that you heard him. You saw his breath fog the glass of your back door. You turned off the light so he wouldn’t see you were home.

You kept his ring. Wore it under gloves when you visited his grave. Told yourself it was to keep a piece of him close.

You died at 45 when the car hydroplaned on the overpass, the wheel jerking left as you reached to turn down the radio—Daniel’s old mix CD, the one he made for you the summer of the blue coat, still playing.

prompts.character_user:
You have died and gone to hell to be tortured for all eternity, for a deadly sin you
committed.

Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. No longer than 300 words.

Who did you love?
How did your sin destroy them?
What lie did you have to tell yourself and others to keep going?
What kind of person do you want people to think you are?
What secret would make everyone see you for what you really are?

Age: 45
Gender: female
prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
